book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan
book.volume: Volume X of The Operating Discipline for AI Library

name: People, Leadership, and Culture
blurb: Researchers interviewed leaders in six Colorado school districts about how they first responded to AI. Some wrote informal guidelines, some banned student use, and some updated their acceptable use policies (McGuire et al., 2026).
title: People, Leadership, and Culture
answer: Researchers interviewed leaders in six Colorado school districts about how they first responded to AI. Some wrote informal guidelines, some banned student use, and some updated their acceptable use policies (McGuire et al., 2026).

papers.why: Gives the book an evidence based frame for the draft then edit pattern: the teacher is both the trainer and the quality check on the tool, which is the human review gate stated as a research finding rather than a policy preference. The nine challenges are a ready made What can go wrong list for Chapters 17 and 20.
papers.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
papers.caveat: Covers 2000 to 2020, so entirely pre ChatGPT. Most included studies used AI to predict outcomes rather than to support live instruction. Only two of the studies involved pre service teachers.
papers.finding: Systematic review of 44 studies (2000 to 2020). AI helps teachers at three points: planning (identifying student needs), implementation (immediate feedback and timely intervention during activities), and assessment (automated scoring). Teachers also serve as the models AI is trained on and as the checkers of AI scoring accuracy. Nine challenges recur: limited algorithm reliability, limited technical capacity (weak on graphics and figures), thin school infrastructure, systems that do not transfer across settings or languages, weak validity in assessment, low teacher technical knowledge, low teacher interest, slow feedback, and feedback that is not adaptive.

papers.why: Gives districts a ready self-assessment for AI PD that covers pedagogy and ethics, not just button-clicking. Confirms PD must pair tool training with teaching strategy.
papers.title: Towards Intelligent-TPACK: An empirical study on teachers’ professional knowledge to ethically integrate artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools into education
papers.caveat: Self-report; Turkish teachers using a national platform (EBA) with chatbot, tutoring, dashboard, and auto-scoring tools; pre-generative AI. Age range reported narrowly (29-38).
papers.finding: Built and validated the Intelligent-TPACK scale (428 Turkish K-12 teachers, EFA and CFA; model tested on a second sample of 400) covering five parts: Intelligent-TK (operating AI tools), Intelligent-TPK (using AI for feedback, monitoring, alerts), Intelligent-TCK (subject-specific AI tools), Intelligent-TPACK (matching AI tool to teaching strategy and goal), and Ethics (judging AI decisions on transparency, fairness, accountability, inclusiveness). Technical knowledge helps teachers judge AI decisions but is not enough on its own; it matters when combined with pedagogical knowledge. Teachers act as orchestrators.

papers.why: Trust, not capability, decides adoption. The two explanation types are a concrete design for any AI PD session in Chapter 20 and for the teacher accuracy check in Chapter 17.
papers.title: Teachers' trust in AI ‐powered educational technology and a professional development program to improve it
papers.caveat: Abstract only. Science teachers and one grading tool; sample size not stated in the abstract.
papers.finding: Experiments with K12 science teachers using an AI grading tool on synthetic and real data. Two explanations reduced teacher concern and raised trust: how the AI makes decisions compared with human experts, and how it complements rather than replaces the teacher. Presents a professional development program and discourse analysis of teachers who completed it.

papers.why: Confirms the gap the book fills in Chapter 3: ethics as judgment, not as a technical explainer. Supports making phronesis (professional judgment) the frame for the human review rule.
papers.title: In search of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy in teacher education: A scoping review
papers.caveat: Abstract only. Scoping review, so it maps the literature rather than testing anything.
papers.finding: Scoping review of 34 papers (2000 to 2023) on AI literacy in teacher education, using episteme, techne, and phronesis as a lens. AI literacy is a growing topic in education but nearly absent in teacher education. Ethics is treated mostly as understanding technical configurations, and teachers' practical and ethical judgment is not captured.

papers.why: The headline statistic for Chapter 20: research and, by extension, district spending goes to tools for students, not to the teachers who must use them.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in teaching and teacher professional development: A systematic review
papers.caveat: Abstract only. Review of research volume, not of effectiveness.
papers.finding: PRISMA review of 95 articles (2015 to 2024). 65 percent study AI in teaching (conversational AI, adaptive learning and assessment, immersive tech, visual and auditory computing, analytics); only 35 percent study AI for teacher professional development. Supply of PD lags demand for AI integration.

papers.why: Shows that AI is already being used to assess teachers themselves (presentations, competency, reflections), which the book must treat as a governance issue in Chapter 20: consent, transparency, and what teacher data a district may analyze. The finding that ethics clearance is rarely mentioned supports the human review and privacy chapter.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Learning Analytics in Teacher Education: A Systematic Review
papers.caveat: Scope is teacher education programs only, not practicing teachers outside them. Covers machine learning and deep learning mainly. The authors note the search cannot guarantee full coverage.
papers.finding: PRISMA review of 30 studies on AI and learning analytics in teacher education. Uses found: visualizing pre service teachers' behaviors and interactions, predicting dropout and risk groups, chatbots that scale mentoring, automatic detection of discourse features in online text, automatic scoring of video recorded oral presentations, intelligent assessment of teaching competency, and classifying written reflections. Most studies used machine learning on behavioral, discourse, and statistical data. Few studies mentioned ethical clearance. Adoption in education is slow compared with medicine, industry, and finance.

papers.why: Ease of use beat usefulness. For Chapter 20, this argues for picking simple tools first and for coaching that connects AI to active learning pedagogy.
papers.title: Influence of Pedagogical Beliefs and Perceived Trust on Teachers’ Acceptance of Educational Artificial Intelligence Tools
papers.venue: International Journal of Human Computer Interaction (Taylor and Francis)
papers.caveat: Abstract only, closed access. Self reported acceptance, not observed use. Korean context.
papers.finding: Survey of 215 teachers in South Korea, structural equation model extending the technology acceptance model. Teachers with constructivist beliefs adopt educational AI tools more than teachers with transmissive beliefs. Perceived usefulness, ease of use, and trust all matter, and ease of use was the strongest predictor of acceptance.

papers.why: Same mechanism as paper 47: use drives acceptance. Supports low stakes hands on exposure as the first PD step.
papers.title: Generative AI and Teachers’ Perspectives on Its Implementation in Education
papers.caveat: Abstract only, no open license. Perceptions; the authors note views may not translate into action.
papers.finding: Survey of 147 teachers on generative AI. Teachers were positive regardless of teaching style; the more often they used GAI, the more positive they became. Teachers believed GAI could support their own PD and be valuable for students.

papers.why: The single strongest finding for Chapter 20: teachers learn AI by using it in class, not by being told about it. This is the research basis for the book's adoption argument that leaders should create low risk chances to apply AI before running ethics briefings, and that training should be practice based and self paced.
papers.title: Developing AI Literacy for Primary and Middle School Teachers in China: Based on a Structural Equation Modeling Analysis
papers.caveat: Non random sample, mostly rural China, one time quantitative survey with no qualitative data. The four dimension instrument is self reported ability, not observed skill.
papers.finding: Survey of 1,013 primary and middle school teachers in China, mostly rural, modeling four AI literacy dimensions: knowing and understanding AI, applying AI, evaluating AI applications, and AI ethics. Applying AI in class is the strongest driver of the other three (path to knowing and understanding AI, beta 0.88), while ethics awareness alone has only a moderate effect (beta 0.17). Better educational background predicts higher literacy. Literacy fell as the grade level taught rose, so elementary teachers scored highest. The authors recommend government policy plus a training design of self paced weekly practice assignments and free choice of study time, with diverse rather than uniform curricula so teacher agency is respected.

papers.why: Two useful cautions for Chapter 6 and 20: using AI more does not make teachers better at detecting AI written work, and understanding, not exposure, drives ethical use.
papers.title: Examining artificial intelligence literacy among pre-service teachers for future classrooms
papers.caveat: Abstract only. Pre service teachers, one university, self report.
papers.finding: Survey of 529 pre service teachers at a Nigerian university with structural equation modeling. Deep AI understanding predicts positive outcomes in use, detection, ethics, creation, and problem solving. No link between AI knowledge and emotion regulation, and active use does not improve ability to detect AI. A trade off exists between applying AI and creating with it.

papers.why: The people who train teachers do not feel ready. Chapter 20 should say so and propose that districts not wait for teacher preparation programs to catch up.
papers.title: The effects of generative AI on initial language teacher education: The perceptions of teacher educators
papers.caveat: Abstract only, NoDerivatives license. 13 participants, one city.
papers.finding: Interviews with 13 English language teacher educators at all four Hong Kong universities offering initial language teacher education. All expect generative AI to change curriculum, instruction, and assessment, but most lack confidence and competence to address it.

papers.why: A tested PD format: direct instruction plus messy case discussion. Fits the book's chapter template of ideas in depth followed by what can go wrong.
papers.title: Enhancing teacher AI literacy and integration through different types of cases in teacher professional development
papers.caveat: Abstract only, NoDerivatives license. Seven teachers, short term.
papers.finding: Case based AI PD program with seven middle school science teachers using three case problems from well structured to ill structured. Teachers drew on personal experience; ill structured cases prompted application of new knowledge. Survey showed a marked rise in AI literacy, mainly in knowing and understanding AI, but teachers applied that knowledge little during case discussions. Authors recommend combining direct instruction with case discussion.

papers.why: Matches paper 38 and 41: teachers trust AI for planning before grading. Chapter 17 should sequence adoption that way.
papers.title: An investigation of teachers' perceptions of using ChatGPT as a supporting tool for teaching and learning in the digital era
papers.caveat: Abstract only, no open license. 40 teachers, private schools, UAE.
papers.finding: Mixed methods with 40 middle and high school teachers in Dubai and Abu Dhabi private schools. Teachers see the most benefit from ChatGPT in lesson planning and teaching activities and less in assessment and feedback. Biggest challenges: bias and accuracy of information and lack of human interaction.

papers.why: Chapter 1 exists because of this finding: plain definitions come first or every later chapter is read through science fiction. Chapter 20's adoption argument gains a mechanism, that fear from misconceptions blocks training, and Chapter 6 gains the integrity concern in teachers' own words.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education: eliciting and reflecting on Swedish teachers' understanding of AI and its implications for teaching & learning
papers.caveat: Small, non random sample from one Swedish region recruited through university networks, though the authors note similar results from German computer science teachers. Pre ChatGPT (data collected 2022, GPT-3 demo).
papers.finding: Questionnaire plus focus groups with Swedish K12 teachers and teacher educators, analyzed with the Intelligent TPACK frame. Teachers' AI knowledge comes from incidental learning and media, so they picture AI as conscious machines or robots, cannot connect algorithms and machine learning to the AI they discuss, and cannot say which competencies belong at which grade. Overestimating AI produces fear, and fear makes some teachers hide AI from pupils and avoid training. Teachers overestimate pupils' digital skill (the digital native myth). Policy and curriculum language on digital competence is vague, so delivery is uneven across municipalities and schools. Surveys understate these gaps; focus groups exposed them. A GPT-3 demo prompted teachers to say out of class assessment will need new methods and to worry about pupils losing the ability to argue in their own words.

papers.why: Gives districts a ready survey to measure staff trust before and after PD, turning adoption readiness into a number. Shows the blocker is not fear of job loss but the sense that AI cannot see the whole child.
papers.title: An Instrument for Measuring Teachers’ Trust in AI-Based Educational Technology
papers.caveat: Single country, science teachers only, 87% female, exploratory factor analysis only (no CFA yet). Scenario was a clustering tool, not generative AI.
papers.finding: Validated a 24-item teacher trust instrument (132 Israeli high-school science teachers, EFA, 7-factor model fit well). Eight dimensions: perceived benefits, lack of human characteristics, lack of transparency, anxieties, self-efficacy, required shift in pedagogy, preferred means to increase trust, AI vs human advice. Teachers rated benefits high (mean 3.8/5) and self-efficacy high (3.8), but trust AI advice less than a peer or expert (2.7). Fear of replacement was low (2.8). Knowing how the tool decides would raise trust (3.7). Lack of human traits (emotion, student history, intuition) was the top reason for distrust (3.5).

papers.why: Principal practices for rolling out AI policy.
papers.title: School principals' technology and transformational leadership practices for spreading the adoption of an artificial intelligence in education (AIED) policy
papers.caveat: Qualitative.
papers.finding: 16 Israeli principals spreading a national AI policy used technology leadership (PD, shared leadership, parent and partner links) and transformational leadership.

papers.why: US district policy evidence.
papers.title: Approaches to Artificial Intelligence Policy Development in K–12 School Districts
papers.caveat: Six districts.
papers.finding: Interviews with six Colorado district leaders: early AI policy relied on informal guidelines, student bans, or updated acceptable use policies; gaps in PD and evaluation.

papers.why: Another teacher AI literacy instrument.
papers.title: Language teachers’ AI literacy: A psychometric study based on the ED-AI framework
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Language teachers.
papers.finding: Psychometric study of language teachers' AI literacy using the ED-AI framework.

papers.why: Echoes Celik and pedagogy-first findings.
papers.title: From proficiency to pedagogy: A mixed-methods study of in-service teachers’ TPACK-GenAI and the mediating role of pedagogical knowledge
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Self-report.
papers.finding: 325 in-service teachers in 26 countries: technological pedagogical knowledge mediated the link from tech skill to overall TPACK-GenAI; confidence came from applying AI to teaching tasks.

papers.why: Pedagogy first, technology second for AI teacher PD.
papers.title: Pedagogy first, technology second: Cross-level relationships between teacher professional knowledge and student learning in artificial intelligence (AI) education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional; one system.
papers.finding: Multilevel study of 46 secondary teachers and 2,832 students. Teacher pedagogical AI knowledge, not technical AI knowledge, predicted students' views of AI for social good and intent to learn AI. Technical knowledge alone slightly lowered social-good views. Neither predicted student AI knowledge directly.

papers.why: Leadership background.
papers.title: Leveraging complex systems: Leading for transformative change
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Conceptual.
papers.finding: Leading transformative change with AI through a complex systems lens.

papers.why: PD evidence in a crisis context.
papers.title: AI literacy in secondary education: framework, assessment, and professional development in the Ukrainian context
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Self-reported gains.
papers.finding: Ukraine: 84% of educators use AI but only 11% know specialized tools; five-level AI literacy framework; PD raised competence 24%.

papers.why: PD planning reference.
papers.title: Enhancing AI literacy for educators: Where to start and to what end?
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Conceptual.
papers.finding: Framework on where to start and what goals to set for educator AI literacy.

papers.why: Teacher prep reference.
papers.title: Preparing pre-service teachers for responsible generative AI use: Curriculum implications for ethics, privacy, and AI literacy
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.caveat: Pre-service.
papers.finding: Curriculum implications for preparing pre-service teachers on GenAI ethics, privacy, and AI literacy.

papers.why: Leader mindset matters for adoption.
papers.title: Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset
papers.caveat: Survey, Germany.
papers.finding: German school leaders: digital mindset (agility, empathy) and ambidextrous leadership predicted AI implementation.

papers.why: Adds African evidence: confidence and seeing AI as useful for social good drive teacher willingness; anxiety is not the main blocker.
papers.title: Teachers’ readiness and intention to teach artificial intelligence in schools
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: Self-report, one country.
papers.finding: Survey of 368 Nigerian in-service teachers (elementary to high school), PLS-SEM. Eight of ten hypotheses supported for readiness and intention to teach AI; confidence, relevance, social good, and attitude mattered. AI anxiety did not significantly affect intention to teach AI.

papers.why: Supports personalized, self-paced teacher PD.
papers.title: A personalized learning system-supported professional training model for teachers' TPACK development
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: No control group reported in abstract.
papers.finding: 161 Thai secondary science teachers improved TPACK in PD with an embedded personalized learning system.

papers.why: Confirms Nazaretsky: teachers trust human advice more. New teachers will not fix this by themselves; training on what models are and when they help is needed.
papers.title: Algorithm appreciation or aversion? Comparing in-service and pre-service teachers' acceptance of computerized expert models
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Swiss sample, judgment tasks not classroom tools, pre-generative AI.
papers.finding: Behavioral and survey study. In-service and pre-service teachers both preferred advice from a human school counselor over an expert model, to a similar degree, so younger teachers are not less algorithm averse. Acceptance depended on task difficulty. In-service teachers lacked knowledge of expert models but thought models could beat humans on some tasks.

children.name: The Core Argument
children.blurb: AI adoption in schools fails or succeeds in predictable ways, and the deciding factor is how people lead it.

children.name: Leaders Who Model Use
children.blurb: Leaders who model AI use show staff that AI is a normal tool with real limits, not something reserved for other people.

children.name: Professional Learning That Works
children.blurb: Professional learning about AI works best when it builds teachers' knowledge of how to teach with AI rather than their technical skill alone.

children.name: Measuring Trust and Knowledge
children.blurb: Districts can measure whether professional learning about AI is actually working by using validated instruments for teachers' trust in AI tools and their knowledge of ethical AI use, called Intelligent TPACK.

children.name: AI Champions in Every Building
children.blurb: An AI champion is a teacher in each school building who uses AI thoughtfully and helps colleagues do the same, so that support sits where teachers actually work.

children.name: Coaching and Evaluation
children.blurb: AI can help instructional coaches and principals turn their observation notes into clearer coaching conversations, but it should not be used to rate teachers through classroom video analysis.

children.name: Hiring and Onboarding
children.blurb: AI can assist with hiring and onboarding tasks such as drafting job postings, organizing applications, scheduling interviews, and answering common new-staff questions, but the decisions about whom to interview and hire stay with people.

children.name: Staff Wellbeing, Time, and Retention
children.blurb: AI is often promoted as a way to cut teacher workload, but the evidence that it actually frees up time is mixed, because saved time tends to be absorbed by other demands unless leaders deliberately decide where it goes.

children.name: Recognition, Meetings, and Communication
children.blurb: Recognition, meetings, and communication are three everyday leadership routines where AI can assist without taking over.

children.name: Strategic Planning and Scenarios
children.blurb: A strategic plan for AI gives a district a clear direction by naming goals tied to student learning and staff time, the rules for AI use, the pilots underway, and how results will be measured.

children.name: A Governance Structure for AI
children.blurb: A governance structure for AI means a standing committee, not a one-time policy, that reviews tools, updates rules, and oversees pilots.

children.name: Staff Voice and Working Conditions
children.blurb: Staff voice and working conditions is the idea that teachers and staff should help shape how AI is introduced into a school, because their concerns about surveillance, evaluation and jobs are legitimate and their knowledge improves adoption.

children.name: Equity Across Schools
children.blurb: Equity across schools means making sure AI adoption does not widen the gap between well-resourced schools and those serving students with the greatest needs.

children.name: Sustaining Change Over Years
children.blurb: Sustaining change over years means building lasting habits of governance, measurement, and honest reporting so that AI adoption survives constant changes in tools and in school leadership.

children.name: An AI Literacy Program for the Whole Community
children.blurb: An AI literacy program for the whole community means that students, teachers and parents all gain some understanding of AI rather than leaving it to a single group.

children.name: The First 90 Days
children.blurb: The First 90 Days is a starting plan for superintendents, principals, teachers, and parents who want to begin using AI in schools without buying new technology.

sections.body: This part of school life is how the adults in a school system take up AI, not the tools themselves. The book describes districts that first responded to AI by writing informal guidelines, banning student use, or updating acceptable use policies, and it notes that nearly all of them had gaps in professional learning and in checking whether their approach worked. It treats AI adoption as a change in how people work, which makes it a question of leadership and culture rather than a technology project. The research it draws on is about how people learn to use AI, and it finds that teaching knowledge matters more than technical skill and that leaders' mindsets shape what happens in their schools.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, as the book describes it, is leaders who model use, published rules, professional learning that builds teacher knowledge and trust, and measures of hours saved and student outcomes rather than licenses and logins. What does not work is performative adoption, where a district announces an initiative, buys licenses, reports rising usage, and leaves governance thin while no one measures results for students, so staff comply on paper and classrooms do not change. The rule the book holds to is that adoption is real only when it changes how the district works, and the evidence for that is a short annual report covering the approved tool list, the human review rule, pilot results with comparison groups, time study results, fairness checks, and measures of teacher trust and knowledge before and after professional learning. The Thirty Day Move follows from that rule: publish the rules, name an AI champion in every building, have every senior leader share one way they use AI, and replace usage based measures with measures of hours saved and student outcomes.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as one argument about people. The Core Argument states the case in full, and Leaders Who Model Use shows why the top of the system sets the tone, while AI Champions in Every Building and A Governance Structure for AI carry that tone into each school and into the rules. Professional Learning That Works, Coaching and Evaluation, and Measuring Trust and Knowledge cover how staff build knowledge and how the district checks whether that knowledge and trust changed, and Hiring and Onboarding, Staff Wellbeing, Time, and Retention, Staff Voice and Working Conditions, Recognition, Meetings, and Communication, and Equity Across Schools cover the working conditions and fairness questions a leader has to answer. Strategic Planning and Scenarios and Sustaining Change Over Years look past the first year, An AI Literacy Program for the Whole Community reaches families and students, and The First 90 Days gives a leader the starting sequence. A teacher would go to the professional learning and coaching pages for what to expect and how they will be supported, a leader would go to the core argument, governance, planning, and the 90 day plan for what to decide and publish, and a parent would go to the community literacy page and the governance page to see what rules apply and what the school is teaching.
